title: Daytime sessions with no rehearsal and little interest in records
summary: Sessions were mostly daytime, tunes were often handed out in the studio without arrangements, and records were just a means of survival.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: So this was a bit unusual, then. Now, when did you usually record? Was it in the daytime or in the evening? What was this kind of a setup?
No, it was mostly in the daytime. Definitely. They were from 9 o'clock in the morning til noon, or from noon until 5 o'clock or something like that. It was strictly daytime recording.

When you had a recording date, was that anything special? Did the band say, 'Look, we've got a recording next week; we're going to have to do these numbers and we're going to have to rehearse'? Or was it just something that you knew the numbers so well you just went in and did them?

No. We didn't know anything so well. We never knew what we was gonna record sometimes until we got in the studio. We never knew what we was gonna record. Sometimes they didn't even have no arrangements on the numbers! Heh-heh. It sounds funny, but it's true.
Some of these sax section parts, though, sound rehearsed.
Yeah. Well, some of them are things that we had been playing. But that was not the majority of the recordings. I mean, that was practically his numbers, where
you'd find (?) arranged in different sections, and this-that-and-the-other. Those were arranged numbers that we had been playing as a band. But now they come up with something new, like this...
Something like "Broadway Rhythm", they must have...

See, that's something altogether new. I mean, we'd walk in the studio and then they'd stick that up in front of you, one of them things, and that's what we're going to record. Well, it was a lot of numbers like that. We never knew what the name of the numbers were even. And we never knew when they were published or anything else, or when they were put out -- we never knew. And we wasn't that much interested in them. All we did was just record them.
And nobody ever bothered to really collect the records.

Oh, no. Nobody wanted that. Some of them, I guess, the majority of the men in the band never even heard in their life. They never heard them. They didn't care much about them. They'd just go in and make the record. It was a date, and then you had to wait for your money two or three months to get paid. It wasn't a big deal. I mean, it wasn't nothin' to get excited about when you made a recording. Because you wasn't gonna get paid that much for the record, and you didn't know how long you were going to have to wait for your money.
Yeah, but I would think you would be wanting to hear what you sound like.
Oh, I could hear myself any day in the week. I could hear myself.
Yeah, except it sounds different when it's just (?) someone else...

There wasn't that much interest out there. I mean, they make a big to-do out of records and sounds, and this-that-and-the-other nowadays. That was a means of existence. That was a means of existence in them days. I mean, a little bit here, and a little bit there, and a little bit of this-that-and-the-other, and all together you might get your rent together. It was tough. I mean, you wasn't thinkin' about no glory in this stuff. It was no glory. You were fightin' for existence. Man, it was tough.
